description: First physics batch: one distinct intuition per question across mechanics, fluids, heat, waves, optics, electromagnetism, relativity and quantum.

defaults.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.
defaults.source: Standard introductory physics (e.g. OpenStax University Physics)

questions.scenario: An astronaut on the Moon holds a hammer in one hand and a feather in the other, at the same height. She lets go of both at the same instant.
questions.question: Which hits the ground first?
questions.reveal: They land together.
questions.explanation: On Earth, air pushes back hard on a feather's big, light surface, so it drifts. The Moon has essentially no atmosphere, so gravity is the only force that matters. A heavier object does feel a stronger pull, but it also has proportionally more mass to get moving, and the two effects cancel exactly. Both speed up at about 1.6 m/s², so they hit the dust at the same moment.
questions.intuitionTrap: Everyday life on Earth is dominated by air resistance, so we learn that heavy things fall faster.
questions.principle: Without air resistance, gravitational acceleration does not depend on the falling object's mass.
questions.funFact: Apollo 15 commander David Scott did exactly this on live TV in 1971, using a falcon feather: a nod to his lunar module, Falcon.

goDeeper.text: The object's own mass m appears in both the gravitational force and its inertia, so it cancels. Every object at the same place falls with the same acceleration.

questions.source: NASA Apollo 15 mission record; standard mechanics

questions.scenario: You throw a ball straight up. At the very top of its flight, for an instant, it isn't moving at all.
questions.question: At that instant, what is the ball's acceleration?
questions.reveal: Still 9.8 m/s², pointing down.
questions.explanation: Velocity and acceleration are different things. At the top, the ball's velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity never switches off, so the ball is still accelerating downward at about 9.8 m/s². That's exactly why it doesn't hover: an instant later its velocity points down. If its acceleration really were zero at the top, it would simply stay there in mid-air.
questions.intuitionTrap: Our brains blur 'not moving' together with 'nothing is changing'.
questions.principle: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; in free flight, gravity supplies a constant downward acceleration.
questions.funFact: Passengers on 'zero-g' training flights float on the way up as well as on the way down: the plane is in free fall for the whole arc, not just the descent.

questions.scenario: A car drives around a perfectly circular track. Its speedometer never moves from 60 km/h.
questions.question: Is the car accelerating?
questions.reveal: Yes, toward the centre of the circle.
questions.explanation: In physics, acceleration means any change in velocity, and velocity includes direction. Going around a circle, the car's direction changes every instant, so it is constantly accelerating toward the centre. That centripetal acceleration is supplied by friction between the tyres and the road. The outward lean passengers feel isn't an outward force on the car; it's their bodies trying to keep going straight while the car turns beneath them.
questions.intuitionTrap: We equate 'accelerating' with 'speeding up', and the outward lean feels like a real outward push.
questions.principle: Velocity is a vector; changing direction at constant speed requires an acceleration of v²/r toward the centre.
questions.funFact: On a curve of 50 m radius at 60 km/h, that centripetal acceleration is more than half of g.

goDeeper.text: At 16.7 m/s on a 50 m radius, a = 16.7²/50 ≈ 5.6 m/s², about 0.57 g. Double the speed and the required acceleration quadruples, which is why fast cornering demands so much grip.

questions.scenario: You stand on a bathroom scale inside an elevator. The doors close and the elevator starts speeding up as it heads upward.
questions.question: While it's speeding up, what does the scale show?
questions.reveal: More than your normal weight.
questions.explanation: A scale measures how hard it pushes up on you. To accelerate you upward, the floor has to push harder than gravity pulls down; the extra push is what speeds you up. So the reading rises. Once the elevator reaches a steady speed, even while still climbing, the reading returns to normal: constant velocity needs no extra force. You feel acceleration, not motion.
questions.intuitionTrap: It's tempting to think 'going up' makes you heavier for the whole ride, but only the speeding-up part does.
questions.principle: Apparent weight = m(g + a): only acceleration changes what a scale reads.
questions.funFact: When the elevator slows to a stop at the top, the reading drops below normal for a moment. Briefly, you weigh less.

goDeeper.equation: N − mg = ma  →  N = m(g + a)
goDeeper.text: With a = 1 m/s² upward, a 70 kg person's scale reading rises from about 70 kg to about 77 kg.

questions.scenario: You're inside a spaceship coasting through deep space with its engines off, far from any planet. You crouch on the floor and push off hard with your legs, as if jumping.
questions.question: What happens next?
options: You rise, slow down and fall back
You glide to the ceiling at steady speed
questions.reveal: You glide to the ceiling at a steady speed.
questions.explanation: With the engines off, you and the ship are both in free fall, so nothing pulls you back toward the floor. When your legs push on the floor, the floor pushes back on you, and you drift toward the ceiling at a constant speed until you hit it. The ship gets a tiny nudge the other way, but it's so massive that its recoil is barely noticeable. To push off you don't need gravity, just something to push against.
questions.intuitionTrap: On Earth every jump ends with a fall, so we expect a return trip.
questions.principle: With no net external force, motion continues in a straight line at constant speed; every push comes with an equal and opposite push.
questions.caveat: If the engines were firing, the ship's acceleration would act like gravity and you would land back on the floor.
questions.funFact: Astronauts on the International Space Station move around exactly like this, gently pushing off the walls with their fingertips.

questions.scenario: A small steel bearing heated to 200 °C is dropped onto a huge iron block at 40 °C. The block stores far more total thermal energy than the little bearing.
questions.question: Which way does heat flow?
options: From the bearing into the block
From the block into the bearing
questions.reveal: From the hot bearing into the big block.
questions.explanation: Heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature, not from 'more energy' to 'less energy'. Temperature reflects how vigorously each particle jiggles; total thermal energy also depends on how much material there is. The block holds more energy overall simply because it's huge, but its particles jiggle less vigorously. Energy moves from the bearing into the block until both reach the same temperature, not the same energy.
questions.intuitionTrap: Confusing temperature (how intense) with heat content (how much).
questions.principle: Heat spontaneously flows from a hotter body to a colder one, whichever holds more total energy.
questions.funFact: A swimming pool at 25 °C holds vastly more thermal energy than a mug of boiling tea, yet if you pour the tea in, heat flows from the tea to the pool.

questions.scenario: A planet has exactly the same mass as Earth, but twice Earth's radius. You stand on its surface.
questions.question: How does your weight compare with your weight on Earth?
options: The same, as the mass is equal
questions.reveal: About a quarter of your Earth weight.
questions.explanation: Gravity weakens with the square of your distance from the planet's centre. Doubling the radius puts you twice as far from the centre, so the pull drops to (½)² = ¼. The planet's mass hasn't changed; you're just standing much farther from it. Such a planet would also be strangely fluffy: the same mass spread through eight times the volume, so one-eighth of Earth's density.
questions.intuitionTrap: If the mass is the same, it feels like gravity should be the same too.
questions.principle: Surface gravity g = GM/r² depends on mass and on the square of the distance from the centre.
questions.funFact: Saturn has about 95 times Earth's mass, yet gravity at its cloud tops is only about 7% stronger than on Earth, because its radius is about 9.5 times larger.
assumptions: The planet is roughly spherical with its mass distributed symmetrically

goDeeper.text: Double r and g falls by 2² = 4. Double M instead and g simply doubles.

questions.scenario: Imagine a magical elevator that carries you 2,000 km straight down into the Earth, about a third of the way to the centre.
questions.question: Compared with standing on the surface, how much do you weigh down there?
questions.reveal: Roughly the same, in fact very slightly more.
questions.explanation: For a planet of uniform density, the answer would be 'less': only the mass beneath you pulls you down, and gravity falls steadily to zero at the centre. But Earth isn't uniform. Its iron core is very dense, so as you descend you leave some rock above you but get much closer to that concentrated mass. Seismic models of Earth's interior show gravity stays close to its surface value through the mantle, rising slightly, and peaks near 10.7 m/s² at the core–mantle boundary.
questions.intuitionTrap: The textbook result, gravity falling steadily with depth, only holds if density is the same everywhere.
questions.principle: Inside a spherically symmetric body only the mass at smaller radius pulls on you, so gravity with depth depends on how density is distributed.
questions.funFact: Gravity only starts falling steeply once you're inside the core, finally reaching zero at the very centre of the Earth.
questions.source: Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), Preliminary Reference Earth Model (PREM)

questions.scenario: You're on a spaceship cruising at 90% of the speed of light. You point a flashlight toward the front of the ship and switch it on.
questions.question: How fast does the beam move away from you, as you measure it?
options: At the full speed of light
questions.reveal: At the full speed of light.
questions.explanation: Light in a vacuum travels at the same speed, c, for every observer moving at constant velocity, however fast they're going. You measure the beam leaving at c. Someone watching from a planet also measures that same beam at c, not 1.9c. What gives way instead is time and distance: the observers' clocks and rulers disagree in exactly the way needed to keep the speed of light the same for both. That single fact is the foundation of special relativity.
questions.intuitionTrap: Everyday speeds simply add up, like a ball thrown forward from a train, so we expect light's speed to add too.
questions.principle: The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers in uniform motion.
questions.funFact: If a ship moving at 0.9c fires a probe forward at 0.9c, an observer on a planet clocks the probe at about 0.994c, not 1.8c.

goDeeper.text: Relativistic velocity addition. Put u′ = c and you get u = c for any v.

questions.scenario: A figure skater is spinning slowly on the ice with her arms stretched wide. She pulls her arms in tight against her body.
questions.question: What happens to her spin?
questions.reveal: She spins faster.
questions.explanation: With very little friction from the ice, her angular momentum stays almost constant. Angular momentum depends on how fast she spins and how far her mass sits from the spin axis. Pulling her arms in moves mass closer to the axis, so she has to spin faster to keep the total the same. It isn't free energy: her muscles do work pulling her arms inward, and that work becomes extra spinning energy.
questions.intuitionTrap: We expect a change in speed to need a push from outside.
questions.principle: Angular momentum (L = Iω) is conserved when no external torque acts.
questions.funFact: A falling cat uses a related trick, tucking and extending its legs at different moments to turn itself over with zero total angular momentum.

questions.scenario: You're sitting in a small rowing boat on a calm pond, holding a heavy rock. You drop the rock over the side and it sinks to the bottom.
questions.question: What happens to the water level of the pond?
questions.reveal: It falls slightly.
questions.explanation: While the rock is in the boat, it pushes the boat deeper, displacing a volume of water that weighs as much as the rock. Rock is roughly two to three times denser than water, so that's two to three times the rock's own volume. Lying on the bottom, the rock displaces only its own volume. Less water is displaced overall, so the pond level drops, just a tiny bit.
questions.intuitionTrap: A splash and a sinking rock feel like they should push the water up.
questions.principle: A floating object displaces its own weight of water; a sunken object displaces only its own volume.
questions.funFact: The same idea explains why a steel ship floats: its hull spreads out so it can push aside a weight of water equal to its own.

questions.scenario: You're underwater in a swimming pool while a friend standing on the edge shouts your name.
questions.question: Why is it so hard to hear them?
options: Most sound bounces off the surface
Sound is much slower in water
questions.reveal: Most of the sound bounces off the water's surface.
questions.explanation: Water is actually a superb carrier of sound: sound travels about four times faster in water than in air, and whale calls can cross hundreds of kilometres. The problem is the boundary. Air and water resist being vibrated very differently (their 'acoustic impedance' differs about 3,600-fold), so roughly 99.9% of the sound energy hitting the surface reflects back into the air. Only a tiny fraction makes it into the pool.
questions.intuitionTrap: Muffled sound suggests water absorbs it, and many people also assume sound is slower in water.
questions.principle: When sound meets a boundary between materials with very different acoustic impedance, most of its energy is reflected.
questions.funFact: Ultrasound scans use a gel between the probe and your skin for the same reason: without it, a thin layer of air would reflect almost all the sound.

questions.scenario: You stand in front of a flat bathroom mirror and can see yourself from the top of your head down to your waist. You walk backwards, away from the mirror.
questions.question: Do you see more of your body?
options: Yes, more of you fits in
questions.reveal: No, exactly the same amount.
questions.explanation: In a flat mirror, your image is as far behind the glass as you are in front of it. Step back and your image shrinks in your view, but the mirror shrinks in your view by exactly the same factor, because both are getting farther from your eye in proportion. So the fraction of your body that fits in the mirror never changes. That's why a flat mirror only needs to be half your height to show you head to toe, from any distance.
questions.intuitionTrap: Things look smaller from far away, so it seems more of you should fit in the frame.
questions.principle: In a flat mirror, the point that reflects your feet into your eyes is always halfway between them in height, wherever you stand.
questions.funFact: Most people predict the opposite even after a lifetime of mirrors. Check it with two sticky notes marking the top and bottom of what you can see.
assumptions: A flat mirror fixed on the wall, with you facing it squarely

questions.scenario: A bird lands on a single bare high-voltage power line carrying thousands of volts, and sits there happily.
questions.question: Why doesn't it get electrocuted?
options: Both feet are at the same voltage
The current moves too fast to enter
questions.reveal: Both its feet are at (almost) the same voltage.
questions.explanation: Current flows through something only when there's a voltage difference across it. Both of the bird's feet grip the same wire a few centimetres apart, so they sit at nearly the same voltage, and that tiny difference pushes almost no current through the bird. The danger comes when a bird or a person touches two different wires, or a wire and something connected to the ground. Then a huge voltage appears across the body.
questions.intuitionTrap: We think of a 'live' wire as dangerous to touch at all, rather than dangerous to bridge.
questions.principle: Current flows only where there is a voltage difference; its size depends on that difference and the resistance.
questions.funFact: Large birds such as eagles are electrocuted surprisingly often because their wingspans can bridge two conductors, so power companies add wider spacing and covers on poles.

questions.scenario: You take a bar magnet, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other, and cut it exactly in half.
questions.question: What do you end up with?
options: A north piece and a south piece
Two magnets, each with N and S
questions.reveal: Two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south pole.
questions.explanation: A bar magnet's magnetism comes from countless atomic-scale magnets, mostly electron spins, lined up together. Cut it anywhere and each piece still contains lined-up atomic magnets, so each gets its own north and south pole. Keep cutting down to single atoms and it's the same story. Nobody has ever found an isolated magnetic 'monopole', a lone north or south, although some theories suggest they could exist.
questions.intuitionTrap: The poles look like separate 'stuff' at each end that could be split apart.
questions.principle: Magnetic poles always come in north-south pairs; no isolated magnetic monopole has ever been observed.
questions.funFact: Physicists have hunted for magnetic monopoles in cosmic rays, Moon rocks and particle colliders, and have found none so far.

questions.scenario: A single bulb glows, connected to a battery. You connect a second identical bulb in parallel, on its own separate path across the same battery.
questions.question: What happens to the brightness of the first bulb?
questions.reveal: It stays about the same.
questions.explanation: In parallel, each bulb has its own path straight across the battery, so each one gets the battery's full voltage. The first bulb's current, and so its brightness, barely changes. What does change is the total current drawn from the battery: it doubles, so the battery runs down about twice as fast. Wire the two bulbs in series instead, one after the other on a single path, and they share the voltage, so both glow dimmer.
questions.intuitionTrap: It feels like two bulbs must 'share' a fixed amount of electricity.
questions.principle: Components in parallel each receive the full source voltage; the source supplies the sum of their currents.
questions.caveat: A real battery has some internal resistance, so drawing more current makes its voltage sag a little and both bulbs dim slightly.
questions.funFact: That's why home sockets are wired in parallel: plugging in a toaster doesn't make the lamps across the room go dim.

questions.scenario: A sealed, perfectly insulated box has gas in its left half and a vacuum in its right half, separated by a thin wall. You remove the wall and the gas rushes to fill the whole box.
questions.question: Once it settles, what has happened to the gas's temperature?
questions.reveal: Unchanged, for an ideal gas.
questions.explanation: Gases cool when they expand by pushing something, like a piston or the air outside a spray can, because they spend energy doing that work. Here the gas expands into empty space, so it pushes against nothing and does no work, and no heat can enter or leave. Its internal energy stays the same, and for an ideal gas internal energy depends only on temperature. So the temperature doesn't change, even though the pressure halves.
questions.intuitionTrap: We associate expanding gas with cooling, like the cold blast from a spray can.
questions.principle: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature; a free expansion does no work and exchanges no heat.
questions.caveat: Real gases change temperature slightly in a free expansion, usually cooling, because their molecules attract each other a little.
questions.funFact: The process only runs one way: the gas never gathers itself back into one half. Its entropy has increased even though its energy hasn't changed.
assumptions: No heat enters or leaves the box

questions.scenario: Two boxes made of the same material, one heavy and one light, slide across the same floor. Both start at the same speed and gradually slow to a stop.
questions.question: Which slides farther?
questions.reveal: They slide the same distance.
questions.explanation: Friction does grow with weight: the heavier box is pressed into the floor harder, so friction pushes back on it harder. But the heavier box also has more mass to slow down. The two effects cancel, so both boxes decelerate at the same rate and stop in the same distance. It's the same cancellation that makes heavy and light objects fall together in a vacuum.
questions.intuitionTrap: Heavy things feel harder to stop, so it seems they should slide farther, or that friction should stop them sooner.
questions.principle: Sliding friction is proportional to the normal force, so the deceleration (μg) does not depend on mass.
questions.funFact: Engineers measure friction this way: tilt a ramp until a block just starts to slide, and the angle reveals the friction coefficient, whatever the block weighs.
assumptions: Simple sliding friction with the same coefficient for both boxes

goDeeper.text: Mass cancels; stopping distance depends only on starting speed and the friction coefficient.

questions.scenario: A heavy truck and a small car collide head-on.
questions.question: During the crash, which vehicle experiences the bigger force?
questions.reveal: Exactly the same force on each.
questions.explanation: Forces always come in pairs: if the truck pushes on the car, the car pushes back on the truck with a force of equal size in the opposite direction, at every instant of the crash. So why is the car wrecked? The same force has very different effects on different masses. The car, with far less mass, undergoes a much larger change in velocity, and its occupants feel much larger accelerations. Equal forces, unequal consequences.
questions.intuitionTrap: Because the car suffers far more damage, we assume it must have felt a bigger force.
questions.principle: Newton's third law: the forces two objects exert on each other are always equal in size and opposite in direction.
questions.funFact: The same is true when you jump: you push Earth down exactly as hard as it pushes you up, but Earth's acceleration is far too tiny to notice.

questions.scenario: Light is fired at a barrier with two narrow slits, but so dimly that only one photon passes through at a time. Each photon makes a single dot on a screen behind.
questions.question: After thousands of photons, what pattern do the dots form?
options: Two bright bands, one per slit
A random, even spray of dots
questions.reveal: Interference stripes, built up one dot at a time.
questions.explanation: Each photon lands at one single spot, like a particle. But as the dots pile up, they build alternating bright and dark stripes, the interference pattern that waves passing through both slits produce. With only one photon in flight at a time there's nothing else for it to interfere with: each photon's probability wave passes through both slits and interferes with itself. Set up a detector to find out which slit each photon used, and the stripes disappear.
questions.intuitionTrap: Interference feels like something that needs many waves, or many photons, mixing together.
questions.principle: Quantum objects propagate as probability waves that can interfere with themselves, yet are detected as individual particles.
questions.funFact: The same experiment has been done with electrons, atoms and even molecules made of hundreds of atoms.

questions.scenario: A radioactive sample has a half-life of one hour. You start with 1 gram of it.
questions.question: How much of the original material is left after two hours?
questions.reveal: A quarter of a gram.
questions.explanation: A half-life doesn't mean 'half now, the other half next time'. It means that in each hour, half of whatever remains decays. After one hour 0.5 g is left; after the second hour, half of that, so 0.25 g. Each atom has a fixed chance of decaying per hour, with no memory of how long it has already waited, so the amount keeps halving and never quite reaches zero.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Half-life' sounds like two halves make a whole, so two half-lives seem like they should finish the job.
questions.principle: Radioactive decay is exponential: each half-life removes half of what remains.
questions.funFact: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, which lets archaeologists date once-living material up to roughly 50,000 years old.

questions.scenario: A proton is made of three quarks held together by gluons. Physicists have measured the masses of those quarks.
questions.question: What fraction of the proton's mass do the three quarks' own masses account for?
questions.reveal: Only about 1%.
questions.explanation: Add up the rest masses of the proton's two up quarks and one down quark and you get only about 1% of the proton's mass. The other 99% is energy: the intense energy of the gluon fields and of the quarks' furious motion inside the proton, which counts as mass through E = mc². So most of the mass of you, your desk and the Earth comes not from the quarks themselves but from the energy of the strong force binding them.
questions.intuitionTrap: We picture mass as the sum of the masses of the parts, as it is for everyday objects.
questions.principle: Mass is a form of energy (E = mc²); in a proton, most of it is the energy of the confined quarks and gluons.
questions.funFact: Electrons get their mass from the Higgs field, but they're so light they make up only about 0.05% of a hydrogen atom's mass.
